source: When in the Southern Fishery, a captured Sperm Whale, after long and weary toil, is brought alongside late at night, it is not, as a general thing at least, customary to proceed at once to the business of cutting him in. For that business is an exceedingly laborious one; is not very soon completed; and requires all hands to set about it. Therefore, the common usage is to take in all sail; lash the helm a’lee; and then send every one below to his hammock till daylight, with the reservation that, until that time, anchor-watches shall be kept; that is, two and two for an hour, each couple, the crew in rotation shall mount the deck to see that all goes well.

But sometimes, especially upon the Line in the Pacific, this plan will not answer at all; because such incalculable hosts of sharks gather round the moored carcase, that were he left so for six hours, say, on a stretch, little more than the skeleton would be visible by morning. In most other parts of the ocean, however, where these fish do not so largely abound, their wondrous voracity can be at times considerably diminished, by vigorously stirring them up with sharp whaling-spades, a procedure notwithstanding, which, in some instances, only seems to tickle them into still greater activity. But it was not thus in the present case with the Pequod’s sharks; though, to be sure, any man unaccustomed to such sights, to have looked over her side that night, would have almost thought the whole round sea was one huge cheese, and those sharks the maggots in it.

Nevertheless, upon Stubb setting the anchor-watch after his supper was concluded; and when, accordingly, Queequeg and a forecastle seaman came on deck, no small excitement was created among the sharks; for immediately suspending the cutting stages over the side, and lowering three lanterns, so that they cast long gleams of light over the turbid sea, these two mariners, darting their long whaling-spades, kept up an incessant murdering of the sharks,* by striking the keen steel deep into their skulls, seemingly their only vital part. But in the foamy confusion of their mixed and struggling hosts, the marksmen could not always hit their mark; and this brought about new revelations of the incredible ferocity of the foe. They viciously snapped, not only at each other’s disembowelments, but like flexible bows, bent round, and bit their own; till those entrails seemed swallowed over and over again by the same mouth, to be oppositely voided by the gaping wound. Nor was this all. It was unsafe to meddle with the corpses and ghosts of these creatures. A sort of generic or Pantheistic vitality seemed to lurk in their very joints and bones, after what might be called the individual life had departed. Killed and hoisted on deck for the sake of his skin, one of these sharks almost took poor Queequeg’s hand off, when he tried to shut down the dead lid of his murderous jaw.

*The whaling-spade used for cutting-in is made of the very best steel; is about the bigness of a man’s spread hand; and in general shape, corresponds to the garden implement after which it is named; only its sides are perfectly flat, and its upper end considerably narrower than the lower. This weapon is always kept as sharp as possible; and when being used is occasionally honed, just like a razor. In its socket, a stiff pole, from twenty to thirty feet long, is inserted for a handle.
“Queequeg no care what god made him shark,” said the savage, agonizingly lifting his hand up and down; “wedder Fejee god or Nantucket god; but de god wat made shark must be one dam Ingin.”

modern_en.title: Chapter 66 — The Shark Massacre
paragraphs: When, in the Southern Fishery, a captured Sperm Whale is brought alongside late at night after long and weary toil, it is not, as a general rule at least, customary to proceed at once to the business of cutting him in. For that business is an exceedingly laborious one; it is not very soon completed, and it requires all hands to set about it. Therefore the common practice is to take in all sail, lash the helm alee, and then send everyone below to his hammock until daylight — with the provision that until then anchor-watches shall be kept; that is, the crew in rotation, two by two, each pair for an hour, shall come up on deck to see that all goes well.

But sometimes, especially on the Line (the Equator) in the Pacific, this plan will not answer at all, because such incalculable hosts of sharks gather around the moored carcass that if it were left so for, say, six hours at a stretch, little more than the skeleton would be visible by morning. In most other parts of the ocean, however, where these fish are not so abundant, their wondrous voracity can at times be considerably reduced by vigorously stirring them up with sharp whaling-spades — a procedure which, nevertheless, in some instances only seems to tickle them into still greater activity. But it was not so in the present case with the Pequod's sharks; though, to be sure, any man unused to such sights who had looked over her side that night would almost have thought the whole round sea was one huge cheese, and those sharks the maggots in it.

All the same, when Stubb set the anchor-watch after finishing his supper, and Queequeg and a forecastle seaman came on deck to keep it, the sharks were thrown into no small uproar. The two men at once hung the cutting stages over the side and lowered three lanterns, which threw long gleams of light across the murky water; then, darting their long whaling-spades, they kept up a ceaseless murdering of the sharks,* driving the keen steel deep into their skulls, which seemed to be their only vital spot. But in the foaming confusion of that tangled, struggling mass, the marksmen could not always hit their target, and this revealed fresh evidence of the enemy's incredible ferocity. The sharks snapped viciously not only at one another's spilled entrails but, bending round like flexible bows, at their own, until those entrails seemed to be swallowed over and over by the same mouth, only to pass out again the opposite way through the gaping wound. Nor was that all. It was dangerous to meddle with the corpses and ghosts of these creatures. A kind of generic or Pantheistic vitality seemed to linger in their very joints and bones after what might be called their individual life had gone. One of these sharks, killed and hauled on deck for its skin, nearly took poor Queequeg's hand off when he tried to shut the dead lid of its murderous jaw.

*The whaling-spade used for cutting-in is made of the very best steel; it is about the size of a man's spread hand, and in general shape corresponds to the garden tool it is named after, except that its sides are perfectly flat and its upper end considerably narrower than the lower. This weapon is always kept as sharp as possible, and when in use it is honed now and then, just like a razor. A stiff pole, from twenty to thirty feet long, is fitted into its socket as a handle.
"Queequeg no care what god made him shark," said the savage, agonizingly lifting his hand up and down. "Whether Fiji god or Nantucket god — but the god that made shark must be one damn Indian."

modern_da.title: Kapitel 66 — Hajmassakren
paragraphs: Når en fanget kaskelot i Sydhavsfangsten sent om natten er bragt ind langs skibssiden efter langt og trættende slid, er det, i hvert fald som regel, ikke skik at gå straks i gang med at skære den op. For det arbejde er overordentlig besværligt. Det er ikke hurtigt overstået, og det kræver, at alle mand tager fat. Derfor er den almindelige fremgangsmåde at tage alle sejl ned, surre roret i læ og så sende alle ned i deres hængekøjer til dagslys — med den forudsætning, at der indtil da holdes ankervagter. Det vil sige, at mandskabet efter tur, to og to, hvert par i en time, kommer op på dækket for at se, at alt er i orden.

Men nogle gange, især på Linjen (Ækvator) i Stillehavet, duer denne plan slet ikke, for der samler sig så utallige skarer af hajer omkring det fortøjede kadaver, at hvis det blev liggende sådan i, lad os sige, seks timer i træk, ville der næsten kun være skelettet at se om morgenen. De fleste andre steder i havet, hvor disse fisk ikke er så talrige, kan deres vidunderlige grådighed dog til tider dæmpes betydeligt ved at ruske kraftigt op i dem med skarpe hvalspader — en fremgangsmåde, som dog i nogle tilfælde kun synes at kilde dem op til endnu større virksomhed. Men sådan var det ikke i dette tilfælde med Pequods hajer. Rigtignok ville enhver, der var uvant med sådanne syn og havde set ud over hendes rælling den nat, næsten have troet, at hele det runde hav var én stor ost, og at hajerne var maddikerne i den.

Alligevel, da Stubb havde sat ankervagten efter sin aftensmad, og Queequeg og en matros fra mandskabsrummet kom op på dækket for at holde den, blev hajerne bragt i ikke ringe oprør. De to mænd hængte straks skæreplatformene ud over siden og firede tre lygter ned, der kastede lange stråler af lys hen over det grumsede vand. Så stak de med deres lange hvalspader og blev ved med at myrde hajerne uden ophør,* idet de drev det skarpe stål dybt ind i deres kranier, som syntes at være deres eneste sårbare sted. Men i den skummende forvirring i den sammenfiltrede, sprællende masse kunne skytterne ikke altid ramme deres mål, og det afslørede nye beviser på fjendens utrolige glubskhed. Hajerne snappede grumt ikke blot efter hinandens udvæltede indvolde, men, idet de bøjede sig rundt som smidige buer, også efter deres egne, indtil indvoldene syntes at blive slugt igen og igen af den samme mund, blot for at passere ud igen den modsatte vej gennem det gabende sår. Og det var ikke alt. Det var farligt at befatte sig med disse væseners lig og spøgelser. En slags almen eller panteistisk livskraft syntes at blive hængende i selve deres led og knogler, efter at det, man kunne kalde deres enkeltliv, var forsvundet. En af disse hajer, som var dræbt og hejst op på dækket for sit skind, rev næsten stakkels Queequegs hånd af, da han forsøgte at lukke dens døde, morderiske kæbes låg.

*Den hvalspade, der bruges til at skære op med, er lavet af det allerbedste stål. Den er omtrent så stor som en mands udstrakte hånd og svarer i almindelig form til det havearbejdsredskab, den er opkaldt efter, bortset fra at siderne er helt flade, og den øverste ende er betydeligt smallere end den nederste. Dette våben holdes altid så skarpt som muligt, og når det er i brug, slibes det nu og da, ligesom en barberkniv. En stiv stang på tyve til tredive fod sættes i dens hylster som skaft.
»Queequeg ligeglad med hvilken gud lave ham haj,« sagde vilden og løftede hånden op og ned i smerte. »Om Fiji-gud eller Nantucket-gud — men gud, der lave haj, må være én forbandet indianer.«
